findings.description: The reports bucket defines no server_side_encryption_configuration, so objects are stored under S3-managed default behavior with no explicit encryption enforcement; the bucket relies on an opt-out default rather than an auditable control, and no KMS key is scoped to the data.
This bucket has no logging block, so no access records are delivered to the audit_trail bucket; activity on the reports archive is unlogged and cannot be audited or investigated after a compromise.
Versioning is not enabled on the reports bucket, so overwritten or deleted objects (including the vendor roster seed object) cannot be recovered and destructive tampering leaves no historical record.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is associated with this bucket, so account- or bucket-level ACLs and policies could expose reports to public access without a hard guardrail preventing it.
The ledger exports bucket has no server_side_encryption_configuration, so financial ledger data is stored without an explicit encryption control or customer-managed key.
No logging block is defined, so access to ledger export objects is not recorded in the audit trail bucket, removing the ability to detect or investigate unauthorized reads of financial data.
Versioning is not enabled on the ledger bucket, so deleted or overwritten ledger exports cannot be restored and tampering with financial records may go undetected.
No public access block resource guards this bucket, leaving the bucket's ACL- and policy-based exposure dependent on optional account-level defaults rather than explicit deny.
The model artifacts bucket has no server_side_encryption_configuration, so model data is stored without enforced encryption at rest or a customer-managed key.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is defined for this bucket, so its exposure is not explicitly constrained against public ACLs or policies.
The runbooks bucket defines no server_side_encryption_configuration, so operational documentation is stored without enforced encryption at rest.
No logging block is defined, so reads and writes against operational runbooks are not recorded in the audit trail.
No public access block is associated with this bucket, so it lacks an explicit safeguard against public ACLs or bucket policies.

The audit trail bucket is configured with acl = "log-delivery-write", which grants the S3 log delivery group WRITE and READ_ACP permissions on the bucket itself; an audit bucket should be append-only via a bucket policy scoped to its log source rather than granting the log delivery group standing ACL rights.
No public access block is declared for the audit trail bucket, so the tamper-evident audit records are not explicitly protected against public ACL or policy exposure.

The seed object is uploaded with no kms_key_id, server_side_encryption, or content settings, so if the destination bucket's default encryption is ever absent the vendor roster is written to S3 without customer-managed encryption.
